1. [Econ 402A L1 Solow Growth Model](note:econ-402a-l1-solow-growth-model) — written notes 1 (law of motion, Solow diagram, shocks, golden rule) and written notes 2 (growth in labor and TFP, stationarizing, level vs growth effects in log paths)
2. [Econ 402A L2 Two-Period Saving Model](note:econ-402a-l2-two-period-saving-model) — saving as a choice: lifetime budget, MRS = 1 + r, smoothing, impatience, market-clearing interest rate, MPK as the return to capital
3. [Econ 402A L3 The Ramsey-Cass-Koopmans Model](note:econ-402a-l3-the-ramsey-cass-koopmans-model) — typed notes (handwritten notes to come): Solow with saving chosen; Euler equation, transversality condition, modified golden rule, competitive equilibrium

4. [Econ 402A L4 Classical Labor Market](note:econ-402a-l4-classical-labor-market) — written notes (typed notes for the discussion and diagram): labor supply from MRS = w/p, labor demand from MPL = w/p, equilibrium at w/p = 20 and 2,000 hours; wage floors, labor taxes, unions
5. [Econ 402A L5 A Search and Matching Model of the Labor Market](note:econ-402a-l5-a-search-and-matching-model-of-the-labor-market) — typed notes (handwritten notes to come): matching function, steady-state unemployment and the Beveridge curve, free-entry vacancy supply, Nash-bargained wages, three-curve equilibrium

[Econ 402A L1 Solow Growth Model](note:econ-402a-l1-solow-growth-model) asks what pins down long-run capital and output per worker. With a fixed saving rate and diminishing returns, [capital accumulates](note:capital-accumulation-equation) until investment just replaces depreciation, at the [Steady State](note:steady-state). It then adds growth in labor and technology, where the steady state moves to capital per effective worker and only technology growth raises the long-run growth rate of output per worker ([Balanced Growth Path](note:balanced-growth-path)). The golden rule shows that the saving rate matters for consumption, but the model simply assumes that rate ([Golden Rule Saving Rate](note:golden-rule-saving-rate)).

[Econ 402A L2 Two-Period Saving Model](note:econ-402a-l2-two-period-saving-model) takes up that gap and makes saving a choice. A consumer facing a lifetime budget sets the [Marginal Rate of Substitution](note:marginal-rate-of-substitution) equal to 1 + r, so saving reflects smoothing, impatience (the [Discount Factor](note:discount-factor)) and the interest rate. With several consumers, [Market Clearing](note:market-clearing) determines r. With capital in the model, the marginal product of capital plays the role of the interest rate, which is the link back to Solow.

[Econ 402A L3 The Ramsey-Cass-Koopmans Model](note:econ-402a-l3-the-ramsey-cass-koopmans-model) joins the two. A planner chooses consumption and capital over many periods ([Ramsey-Cass-Koopmans Model](note:ramsey-cass-koopmans-model)): the [Consumption Euler Equation](note:consumption-euler-equation) now prices saving at the return on capital net of depreciation, the [Transversality Condition](note:transversality-condition) closes the infinite horizon, and the steady state sets the marginal product of capital to $1/\beta - 1 + \delta$. That modified golden rule leaves capital and the saving rate below the [golden rule](note:golden-rule-saving-rate) whenever the planner is impatient, and competitive markets reach the same outcome.

[Econ 402A L4 Classical Labor Market](note:econ-402a-l4-classical-labor-market) turns from capital to labor. Workers trade leisure for consumption until the [Marginal Rate of Substitution](note:marginal-rate-of-substitution) equals the real wage ([Labor-Leisure Choice](note:labor-leisure-choice)); firms hire until the marginal product of labor equals it ([Labor Demand](note:labor-demand)). The real wage clears the market ([Classical Labor Market Model](note:classical-labor-market-model)), so unemployment needs something that holds the wage up, such as a wage floor or a union, and a labor tax lands the same way whoever pays it ([Tax Incidence](note:tax-incidence)).

[Econ 402A L5 A Search and Matching Model of the Labor Market](note:econ-402a-l5-a-search-and-matching-model-of-the-labor-market) replaces the single market-clearing wage with search. A [Matching Function](note:matching-function) turns unemployed workers and vacancies into hires; inflows and outflows settle at a [Steady-State Unemployment Rate](note:steady-state-unemployment-rate) that falls with tightness, which is the [Beveridge Curve](note:beveridge-curve). Free entry of vacancies and [Nash Bargaining](note:nash-bargaining) over wages pin down tightness, so unemployment exists in equilibrium ([Diamond-Mortensen-Pissarides Model](note:diamond-mortensen-pissarides-model)).

So far the course moves from a mechanical saving rule to the optimizing behavior behind it. Both lectures use [Partial Derivatives and the Gradient](note:partial-derivatives-and-the-gradient); L1's golden rule is an [Unconstrained Optimization](note:unconstrained-optimization), and L2's consumer problem uses [Constrained Optimization and Lagrange Multipliers](note:constrained-optimization-and-lagrange-multipliers) (see the math refresher below).

[Math Prep](note:math-prep) — especially logs and growth rates ([Math Prep L7 Approximations Logs and Series](note:math-prep-l7-approximations-logs-and-series)), homogeneity and partial derivatives ([Math Prep L4 Multivariable Differentiation](note:math-prep-l4-multivariable-differentiation)) and optimization ([Math Prep L6 Optimization](note:math-prep-l6-optimization)).
